title: Minyeides
titleEn: The Daughters of Minyas — Metamorphoses IV.1–54
source: P. Ovidius Naso, Metamorphoses, ed. Hugo Magnus (Gotha: F.A. Perthes), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-latinLit phi0959.phi006.perseus-lat2, sha256 fb3fdb1d8a4a3b82. Collated against The Latin Library (cltk mirror) as a disagreement detector only. Original spelling kept. Pronunciation convention: reconstructed Classical (restored) Latin, applied consistently. All translations were made fresh from the Latin for Lectorium.
about: Alcithoë and her sisters refuse to accept the rites of Bacchus, denying that he is the son of Jupiter, while the god's priest orders the festival kept and sends the women of the household, servants and mistresses alike, out in the god's dress with garlands and thyrsi; the women of Thebes call on Bacchus under a long string of cult names. The sisters stay indoors at their wool and their looms, and to lighten the day's work they agree to tell one another stories in turn. The first of them runs through several tales she might tell before settling on the one about a tree whose white fruit turned black.

advisory.lede: At line 21 the poem calls India decolor, "discoloured" — a Roman epithet that describes dark skin as a departure from a norm.
advisory.more: decolor is de-, "away from", plus color: out of its colour, off-colour. Roman poets used it as a standing epithet for the peoples of India and of the far south and east, and the norm it measures them against is a paler skin. It carries no argument here — the word sits in a list of the lands Bacchus is hymned for conquering, and Ovid did not coin it — but it describes living peoples by their colour, and it reads as a racial description now. Lectorium presents the text unaltered, as written; the translation keeps the word rather than a modern neutral one, and the note on the line explains it where it stands.

sentences.t:
At non Alcithoe Minyeias orgia censet
accipienda dei, sed adhuc temeraria Bacchum
progeniem negat esse Iovis, sociasque sorores
inpietatis habet.
sentences.l: But Alcithoë, daughter of Minyas, does not judge that the god's rites are to be received; instead, still reckless, she denies Bacchus to be the offspring of Jove, and has her sisters as partners of her impiety.
sentences.i: But Alcithoë, Minyas's daughter, does not think the god's rites should be accepted at all; rash as ever, she denies that Bacchus is Jupiter's son, and she has her sisters in on the impiety with her.
sentences.n: Three things at once, and all three recur constantly in Ovid. (1) `censet orgia accipienda [esse]` is a gerundive inside an indirect statement — literally "she judges the rites to be needing-to-be-received", where English wants "she does not think the rites should be accepted". (2) `negat esse` — Latin says "she denies him to be" where English says "she denies that he is". (3) `Minyeias` is a patronymic adjective, "the Minyas-daughter"; Latin verse names women this way constantly and the reader is expected to supply the father. `socias sorores inpietatis` uses `socius` with the genitive — "sisters who share in the impiety". `adhuc` is temporal: she has been told, and still says it. Two word-choices worth pinning down: `censet` is a verb of judgement, the word used of the Senate voting an opinion, so what is negated is her view of the matter and not her will — she does not *think* the rites should be taken up; and `temeraria` is "rash, heedless, acting without reckoning", not knowing defiance. Both matter, because it is holding a wrong opinion that makes her impious rather than merely obstructive.

sentences.t:
Festum celebrare sacerdos
inmunesque operum famulas dominasque suorum
pectora pelle tegi, crinales solvere vittas,
serta coma, manibus frondentes sumere thyrsos
iusserat,
sentences.l: The priest had ordered the maidservants and their mistresses, exempt from tasks of their own, to celebrate the festival, to be covered as to their breasts with a hide, to loosen their hair-bands, [to take] garlands in their hair, to take up leafy thyrsi in their hands,
sentences.i: The priest had ordered the servants and their mistresses alike, released from their own work, to celebrate the festival, cover their breasts with a skin, unbind their hair-ribbons, put garlands in their hair and take up leafy thyrsi in their hands,
sentences.n: Watch how long the sentence hangs: everything from `Festum` onward waits on the verb `iusserat`, which does not arrive until the fifth line. Latin can suspend like this because the case-endings hold the pieces in place; English cannot, so the translation has to give the verb early and let the list follow. `pectora pelle tegi` is the **Greek accusative of respect** — `pectora` is not what is covered grammatically but the part with respect to which the women are covered: "covered *as to* their breasts with a skin". You will meet this all through the poem, especially with passive and deponent participles. `inmunes operum ... suorum` is `inmunis` + genitive, "free from". The thyrsus is the Bacchic wand: a stalk wound with ivy and topped with a pine-cone. `serta coma` has no verb of its own and borrows `sumere` from the next clause. One more thing to see in the list: of the infinitives hanging on `iusserat` only `tegi` is passive — `celebrare`, `solvere` and `sumere` are all active, and `famulas dominasque` are the accusative subject of the whole string, `celebrare` included. That is why `pectora` can be an accusative of respect in the one passive clause and nowhere else, and it is why "the festival was ordered to be celebrated" would be the wrong shape: the women are ordered to celebrate it.

sentences.t:
et saevam laesi fore numinis iram
vaticinatus erat.
sentences.l: and he had prophesied that the anger of the slighted divine power would be savage.
sentences.n: `fore` is the alternative future infinitive of `sum` (= `futurum esse`), very common in verse because it is short. `numen` is not "god" as a person but the god's power and will — the nod of the head that makes something so; "the slighted godhead" is nearer than "the offended god". `laesi` is the ordinary verb for injuring a divinity by neglect. The priest's warning is a piece of narrative machinery: everything that happens to these sisters is now announced in advance.

sentences.t:
Parent matresque nurusque
telasque calathosque infectaque pensa reponunt,
turaque dant Bacchumque vocant Bromiumque Lyaeumque
ignigenamque satumque iterum solumque bimatrem:
sentences.l: They obey — matrons and young wives alike — and put away their looms and their wool-baskets and their unworked portions of wool; they give incense and call on Bacchus, and Bromius, and Lyaeus, and the fire-born, and the twice-begotten, and the only one with two mothers:
sentences.i: They obey, mothers and daughters-in-law together, and set aside looms, wool-baskets and half-spun wool; they burn incense and call him Bacchus, Bromius, Lyaeus, the fire-born, the twice-sown, the only one born of two mothers:
sentences.n: Count the `-que`s: twelve in four lines — two, three, four, three. The piling is deliberate — it reproduces the sound of a cult litany, where the god is called by name after name in one breath. English keeps some of it with "and ... and ..." and has to let the rest go. The titles: `Bromius` "the roarer", `Lyaeus` "the looser" (of care), `ignigena` "fire-born" because his mother Semele was destroyed by Jupiter's lightning while carrying him, `satus iterum` "sown a second time" and `bimater` "two-mothered" because Jupiter then carried him to term sewn into his own thigh. Note also what they put down — `telas`, `calathos`, `pensa`. It is the same work the Minyeides refuse to put down at lines 34–35, where the loom (`telae`) comes back by name and the wool and thread with it; the parallel is one of activity rather than of vocabulary. `infecta` is `in-` + `factus`, "not made up", i.e. still unspun. Watch the tense floor drop here too. The priest's orders stood in the pluperfect (`iusserat`, `vaticinatus erat`) — finished before the scene starts — and from `Parent` onward everything is present: obey, put away, give, call. Latin verse moves between these constantly, the present bringing the reader inside the action and the perfect or pluperfect standing back from it, and the whole hymn that follows stays in the present.

sentences.t:
additur his Nyseus indetonsusque Thyoneus,
et cum Lenaeo genialis consitor uvae,
Nycteliusque Eleleusque parens et Iacchus et Euhan,
et quae praeterea per Graias plurima gentes
nomina, Liber, habes.
sentences.l: To these is added Nyseus, and unshorn Thyoneus, and, together with Lenaeus, the fruitful planter of the grape, and Nyctelius and father Eleleus and Iacchus and Euhan, and all the very many names besides which you bear among the peoples of Greece, Liber.
sentences.i: To these are added Nyseus and long-haired Thyoneus, and, with Lenaeus, the planter who makes the vine bear, and Nyctelius and father Eleleus, Iacchus and Euhan — and all the other names, so many of them, that you go by among the peoples of Greece, Liber.
sentences.n: **Apostrophe**: the list of names slides, without warning, into direct address — `habes`, "you have". Ovid turns aside to speak to his characters and his gods constantly, and it is worth noticing each time, because the second person can arrive in the middle of a sentence that began in the third. `additur` is singular, agreeing with the nearest of its several subjects — normal Latin, wrong-looking English — and it is passive with no agent named: the poem does not say who adds these names, and English should not supply a "they". The hymn is already drifting from the women at their incense toward the poet's own catalogue, which is what lets it slide into direct address (`habes`) three lines on. `cum Lenaeo` adds Lenaeus as one item of the list and `genialis consitor uvae` is a further title beside him, not a gloss on him — the roll-call's whole point is its length, so a name folded into an apposition is a name lost. `genialis` is not English "genial": it belongs to `genius` and means generative, fruitful, festive. `indetonsus` "unshorn" marks the god's uncut hair, the sign of a youth who never ages. `Liber` is the old Roman god of growth and wine whom the Romans identified with Bacchus, so the Greek roll-call ends on his Latin name.

sentences.t:
Tibi enim inconsumpta iuventa est,
tu puer aeternus, tu formosissimus alto
conspiceris caelo, tibi, cum sine cornibus adstas,
virgineum caput est.
sentences.l: For to you there is a youth never used up; you are the everlasting boy, you are looked upon as most beautiful in the high heaven; and to you, when you stand without your horns, there is a maidenly head.
sentences.i: For your youth is never spent; you are the boy who never ages, and in the high heaven you are seen as the loveliest of all; and when you stand there without your horns, your head is a girl's.
sentences.n: **Dative of possession**, twice: `tibi ... iuventa est` and `tibi ... caput est`, literally "to you there is a youth / a head". Latin says the thing exists *for* the owner; English says the owner has it. It is worth translating literally once, as here, to see the shape. `conspiceris` is second-person passive, "you are gazed on", with `formosissimus` predicative — not "you look at" but "you are looked at". The horns are Bacchus's: he is shown horned as a bull-god, and Ovid's point is that without them he could be taken for a girl — the god's beauty is deliberately androgynous, and the poem says so flatly.

sentences.t:
Oriens tibi victus, adusque
decolor extremo qua tingitur India Gange:
sentences.l: The East has been conquered by you, right up to where discoloured India is dyed by the farthest Ganges:
sentences.i: You have conquered the East, all the way to the place where discoloured India is steeped by the Ganges at the world's edge:
sentences.n: `decolor` means literally "off-colour, out of colour, discoloured" — the prefix marks a departure from a norm, and the norm assumed is a paler skin. Applied to a people it means "dark-skinned", and it is the conventional epithet Roman poets use for the peoples of the far east and south; it is a fixed descriptive tag of the period, not something Ovid invents for this line. Both layers keep "discoloured" rather than a modern neutral word for complexion: the departure-from-a-norm is the whole of what the Latin says, and a reader is owed the word itself rather than an interpretation of it. It belongs to the ancient text's picture of the world, not to the translation, which renders what the Latin says. Grammar: `tibi` is a dative of agent — the ordinary construction with a gerundive, which verse extends to the perfect passive as here (`victus [est] tibi`, "has been conquered by you"), where prose would say `a te`; `adusque ... qua` = "all the way to the point where"; `tingitur` is "is wetted, dipped, dyed", the dyer's verb, and set beside `decolor` it lets a colour-word answer a colour-word — which is why the literal says "is dyed" and not "is washed".

sentences.t:
Penthea tu, venerande, bipenniferumque Lycurgum
sacrilegos mactas, Tyrrhenaque mittis in aequor
corpora, tu biiugum pictis insignia frenis
colla premis lyncum;
sentences.l: You, one who must be revered, slaughter Pentheus and axe-bearing Lycurgus, sacrilegious both, and send Tyrrhenian bodies into the sea; you press down the paired necks of lynxes, conspicuous with painted reins;
sentences.i: You, who must be revered, make sacrificial victims of Pentheus and Lycurgus of the double axe, sacrilegious men both, and send the Tyrrhenian crew into the sea; you rein in the yoked necks of your lynxes, gleaming under their painted harness;
sentences.n: `mactas` is the verb used of slaughtering a sacrificial victim, not of plain killing: the men who profaned the god's rites are themselves made into offerings, and the word is chosen for that — so both layers keep the altar in view rather than falling back on ordinary battle language. `mittis` beside it is the plain verb "you send", and the English should stay as flat as the Latin: the violence of the Tyrrhenian episode is left to the reader. `sacrilegos` stands predicatively — you kill them *as* sacrilegious men — which is where their guilt is stated. `Penthea` is a Greek accusative singular (`Pentheus`, acc. `Penthea`); Greek names keep Greek endings all through this poem. `venerande` is a gerundive in the vocative, "you who are to be worshipped", a hymn formula. `biiugum` is a contracted genitive plural (= `biiugorum`) going with `lyncum`, "of the lynxes yoked in pairs". The Tyrrhenian bodies are the pirate crew turned into dolphins.

sentences.t:
bacchae satyrique sequuntur,
quique senex ferula titubantes ebrius artus
sustinet et pando non fortiter haeret asello.
sentences.l: Bacchants and satyrs follow, and that old man who, drunk, holds up his tottering limbs with a fennel-stalk and clings none too firmly to his sway-backed little donkey.
sentences.i: Bacchants and satyrs come behind, and the drunken old man who holds his tottering legs up on a fennel-stalk and clings none too stoutly to his swaybacked little donkey.
sentences.n: `quique` is a relative with its antecedent left out — "and [the one] who ..." — and the whole clause is a second subject of `sequuntur`: the bacchants and satyrs follow, and so does the old man who props his tottering limbs on a fennel-stalk. Do not confuse it with the **connecting relative**, which is a relative pronoun opening a whole new sentence where English opens with "and he", "and she"; that one you meet at line 36, `E quibus una`. The old man is Silenus, Bacchus's tutor. He is not named in these lines — the donkey and the drunkenness identify him at once — though Ovid does name him elsewhere in the poem. `non fortiter` is **litotes**, saying less than is meant for effect — "not stoutly" is a polite way of saying he is barely staying on. `ferula` is the giant fennel, whose light hollow stalk is the Bacchic staff; `asello` is a diminutive, and `pando` "curved, swaybacked" makes the animal as decrepit as the rider.

sentences.t:
Quacumque ingrederis, clamor iuvenalis et una
femineae voces inpulsaque tympana palmis
concavaque aera sonant longoque foramine buxus.
sentences.l: Wherever you go, a youthful shout, and women's voices along with it, and drums struck by palms, and hollow bronze sound out, and the boxwood with its long bore.
sentences.i: Wherever you go, young men's shouting and women's voices with it, drums beaten with the flat of the hand, hollow bronze cymbals and the long-bored boxwood pipe all sound together.
sentences.n: Two instruments are named by the stuff they are made of: `aera` "bronzes" are cymbals, and `buxus` "boxwood" is the pipe turned from it. This metonymy is a settled habit of Latin verse, and once you see it you will meet it everywhere — the material stands for the object, the object for its use. `una` here is the adverb "together, at the same time", not a form of "one". `sonant` is plural because the subjects are many, even though the first of them (`clamor`) is singular. The second-person address to the god is still running: `ingrederis`.

sentences.t:
“Placatus mitisque” rogant Ismenides “adsis,”
iussaque sacra colunt.
sentences.l: "Appeased and gentle," the daughters of Ismenus beg, "be present with us," and they tend the rites they were ordered to keep.
sentences.i: "Come to us appeased and gentle," the Theban women pray — and they keep the rites they were ordered to keep.
sentences.n: `adsis` is the technical word of prayer: a god is asked to *be there*, present at his own rite, and the subjunctive is a wish, not a command. Note that `rogant` takes the wish-clause with no `ut` at all — normal in verse. `placatus mitisque` are predicative adjectives attached to `adsis`: not "be appeased" but "be here, appeased". `Ismenides` are the women of Thebes, named from the Theban river Ismenus, exactly as `Minyeias` named Alcithoë from her father. `iussa sacra` picks up `iusserat` from the priest's order twenty-four lines earlier: these women did as they were told, and the line puts that in one word.

sentences.t:
Solae Minyeides intus
intempestiva turbantes festa Minerva
aut ducunt lanas, aut stamina pollice versant,
aut haerent telae famulasque laboribus urgent.
sentences.l: Only the daughters of Minyas, indoors, disturbing the festival with untimely Minerva, either draw out the wool, or turn the threads with a thumb, or stay stuck at the loom and press their maidservants with work.
sentences.i: Only Minyas's daughters stay indoors, spoiling the holiday with out-of-season weaving: they draw out wool, or twist the thread under the thumb, or keep at the loom and drive their servants at the work.
sentences.n: `Minerva` here means wool-work — spinning and weaving are her craft, so the goddess's name stands for it, the same metonymy as `aera` and `buxus` above but with a god instead of a material. The sentence is built on the collision: they disturb one god's festival by serving another goddess at the wrong hour, and `intempestiva` "out of due season" carries the whole charge. `ducere lanas` is the technical phrase for drawing the wool out into a strand; `stamina versare pollice` is twisting it into thread. `haerent telae` takes a dative, "cling to the loom". The three `aut`s make one long refusal.

sentences.t:
E quibus una levi deducens pollice filum
“dum cessant aliae commentaque sacra frequentant,
nos quoque, quas Pallas, melior dea, detinet” inquit,
“utile opus manuum vario sermone levemus:
sentences.l: One of them, drawing the thread down with a light thumb, says: "While the others are idle and throng to made-up rites, let us too, whom Pallas, the better goddess, keeps here, lighten the useful work of our hands with talk of one thing and another:
sentences.i: One of them, drawing the thread down under a light thumb, said: "While the rest do nothing and crowd to those invented rites, let us — kept here by Pallas, the better goddess — make the useful work of our hands lighter with a bit of talk:
sentences.n: The contempt in this speech is the speaker's, not the poem's, and the translation keeps it at her pitch. `commenta sacra` means "invented, fabricated rites" — she is calling the whole festival a fiction; `cessant` says the rest of the city is loafing; and `melior dea` "the better goddess" ranks Minerva over Bacchus to his face. Ovid does not endorse any of it, and the priest's prophecy at line 8 is still standing. Grammar: `levemus` is a hortatory subjunctive, "let us lighten"; `E quibus una` is the **connecting relative** proper — a relative pronoun opening a whole new sentence where English opens with "and one of them" (the `quique` at line 26 was a different thing, a relative with its antecedent left out). `inquit` sits inside the quotation rather than in front of it, and that is where Latin normally puts a verb of saying: `inquit` is postpositive and never stands first in its clause. Note too that `inquit` is present in form, and so is the narrative around it (`ducunt`, `versant`, `haerent`, then `probant`, `iubent`), while the idiomatic English drops into the past — English narrative will not carry a present tense this long. That gap between the two layers is the historic present showing. `nos quoque` is the plain adverb "we too" — but keep an eye on `quoque`, which is sometimes `quō-que`, "and by which".

sentences.t:
perque vices aliquid, quod tempora longa videri
non sinat, in medium vacuas referamus ad aures.”
sentences.l: and by turns let us bring out into the middle, for ears that have nothing to do, something that will not let the hours seem long."
sentences.i: and let us take turns telling, for ears with nothing else to occupy them, some story that keeps the hours from dragging."
sentences.n: `in medium referre` is the idiom for laying something before the company — "into the middle", into the shared space of the room. `vacuas ... aures` are ears "at leisure, unoccupied", and the phrase is the whole conceit of this frame: the hands are busy at the wool, so the ears are free for stories. `quod ... non sinat` is a relative clause of characteristic, with the subjunctive: not "which does not allow" but "of the sort that would not allow" — she is describing a kind of story, not a particular one. `per vices` "by turns" is the rule they set themselves, and it is the frame the stories that follow are told inside: each sister takes her turn while the wool keeps moving.

sentences.t: Dicta probant primamque iubent narrare sorores.
sentences.l: The sisters approve the things said, and bid her, as the first one, tell a tale.
sentences.i: Her sisters approve, and tell her to be the one to begin.
sentences.n: `dicta` is a perfect participle used as a plain noun, "the things said" — Latin does this constantly and English has to expand it ("what she had said"). `primam` is an adjective agreeing with the unexpressed accusative subject of `narrare`, i.e. with her: literally "they bid her, first, to tell". Latin prefers an adjective where English reaches for an adverb, and "tell first" is what it comes to. `iubeo` takes accusative + infinitive, not a `ut` clause.

sentences.t:
Illa, quid e multis referat (nam plurima norat),
cogitat et dubia est, de te, Babylonia, narret,
Derceti, quam versa squamis velantibus artus
stagna Palaestini credunt motasse figura;
sentences.l: She turns over which one out of many she should tell (for she knew a great many) and is in doubt — whether she should tell of you, Babylonian Dercetis, whom the people of Palestine believe to have stirred the pools, her shape changed, with scales veiling her limbs;
sentences.i: She thinks over which of the many stories to tell — she knew a great many — and cannot decide: whether to tell of you, Dercetis of Babylon, whom the people of Palestine believe stirred their pools once her shape was changed and scales had covered her limbs;
sentences.n: Another **apostrophe**, and a strange one: the poem turns to address Dercetis directly inside a list of stories that are *not* going to be told. `quid ... referat` and `narret` are deliberative subjunctives in indirect question — "which is she to tell?", "is she to tell of...?" — and the second has no conjunction at all, which is why it can be read straight past. `norat` is syncopated for `noverat` and `motasse` for `motavisse`; verse drops these syllables freely. `versa ... figura` is an **ablative absolute** — a self-contained "with her shape turned" where English wants a clause — and its two words are prised a line and a half apart, `versa` in the middle of the first line and `figura` at the very end of the second, with everything between them held inside it: the second ablative absolute `squamis velantibus artus` and the main verb `credunt motasse` alike. `Palaestini` are the inhabitants of the coastal strip the Romans called Palaestina, the country around Ascalon where Dercetis — the Syrian fish-goddess Atargatis — was worshipped; it is a Roman geographical adjective and not a modern nationality.

sentences.t:
an magis, ut sumptis illius filia pennis
extremos albis in turribus egerit annos;
sentences.l: or rather how her daughter, with wings taken on, passed her final years in white towers;
sentences.i: or rather how her daughter took wings and spent her last years in white towers;
sentences.n: `ut` with the subjunctive here means "how", introducing an indirect question, not "so that" — the sense is fixed by `narret` still governing from two lines back. `sumptis ... pennis` is another ablative absolute, the second in as many units, and English turns it into a finite verb ("took wings"). `annos agere` is the idiom for passing one's years. The daughter is Semiramis; the white towers are dovecotes, and the bird is a dove — Ovid names neither, and expects the reader to work it out from the towers.

sentences.l: or how a water-nymph, with her singing and with herbs too powerful, turned young men's bodies into silent fish, until she suffered the same thing herself;
sentences.i: or how a water-nymph, with her singing and with herbs that worked better than she meant them to, turned young men into silent fish — until the same thing was done to her;
sentences.n: `an ut` continues the chain of indirect questions still hanging on `narret` in line 44 — three tales offered and refused before one is taken. `tacitos` "silent" is doing real work: fish were the proverbially voiceless creatures, so the punishment takes the young men's voices as well as their shape. `nimium potentibus` "too powerful" is dry: the herbs worked better than she meant them to. `donec` takes the indicative here because the clause states a plain fact of time, not a purpose. The nymph is left unnamed, and the story stays a title.

sentences.t:
an, quae poma alba ferebat,
ut nunc nigra ferat contactu sanguinis arbor.
sentences.l: or how the tree which used to bear white fruit now bears black, from the touch of blood.
sentences.n: The antecedent `arbor` is held back to the last word of the line while its own relative clause comes first — a Latin order English cannot copy, so the translation has to lead with "the tree". Watch the tenses: `ferebat` imperfect for what the tree used to do, `ferat` present subjunctive (indirect question) for what it does now, with the change of colour sitting between them. `contactu sanguinis` is an ablative of cause, "by the touching of blood". This is the tale she chooses, and the poem announces it here by its outcome alone, without a name.

sentences.t:
Hoc placet, hanc, quoniam vulgaris fabula non est,
talibus orsa modis, lana sua fila sequente:
sentences.l: This pleases them; and this story, since the tale is not a common one, she having begun in such strains, her wool following out its own thread:
sentences.i: This is the one they like; and since the story is not one everybody tells, she began it in words like these, her wool running out its thread as she spoke:
sentences.n: `hoc` is neuter and `hanc` feminine, a line apart and both pointing at the same tale: the neuter picks up the matter in hand — this is the one to tell — while `hanc` has been drawn into agreement with an unexpressed `fabulam` and is the object of `orsa [est]`. The shift is grammatical, not a change of subject, and the literal keeps it visible rather than levelling both to "this one". The sentence has no finite main verb: `orsa` is the perfect participle of the deponent `ordior` "begin", and its `est` is simply left out, so the line hangs open and runs straight on into the tale itself. `vulgaris` means "common, in everybody's mouth" — her reason for choosing this one is that it is *not*. `talibus ... modis` is "in such measures", with a glance at verse. `lana sua fila sequente` is one last ablative absolute, and it is the image the whole frame rests on: the thread keeps paying out while the story is told, work and telling going forward together.

questions: IV.18 `tu puer aeternus` is a short, quotable tag and is on neither house-rendering list. Shipped as literal "you are the everlasting boy" and idiomatic "you are the boy who never ages", built from the Latin (`tu` + predicate noun, verbless, inside the run of second-person address that starts at `habes` in line 17). Recorded here for ratification as a house rendering rather than re-decision in a later batch.

The advisory over `decolor` at IV.21 was kept and shipped in object form under trigger 1. The word is a standing poetic epithet, not an aetiology of a people's body, so the trigger as written in `content-advisory.md` does not squarely cover it; it was applied on the trigger's purpose — offence landing on a present-day group — which it meets as squarely as ovid-met-011's line about the Ethiopians. This is the first standing epithet of colour in the poem to be flagged and it should be ratified as a rule before `niger`, `fuscus` and the rest arrive.

The `more` paragraph says the word "reads as a racial description now", which is a step past the previous copy's describe-the-convention-and-stop. House style requires the paragraph to say the thing is offensive now; the line between saying it plainly and lecturing is the one the style file warns about, and the tone should be confirmed once for the whole class of epithets rather than per part.
